question: What is the main goal of giving a vaccine?

options.A: To replace missing white blood cells
options.B: To flush waste products out of the blood
options.C: To help the body build its own defense against a specific germ
options.D: To provide quick relief from an active bacterial infection

explanation: Vaccines introduce harmless parts of a germ so the body can learn to fight it without getting sick. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h1)

question: How does herd immunity help protect vulnerable people in a community?

options.A: By lowering how much a disease spreads among people
options.B: By passing antibodies through breast milk
options.C: By creating a chemical barrier on the skin
options.D: By curing chronic infections in sick patients

explanation: When most people are vaccinated, it is hard for a disease to find a new host, which indirectly protects those who cannot take vaccines. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h1)

question: Which type of vaccine uses a weakened, live version of the germ?
explanation: Live-attenuated vaccines contain a weakened form of the live germ that grows poorly in the body but teaches the immune system well. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h2)

question: Why do inactivated (killed) vaccines usually need booster shots?

options.A: They break down quickly in the liver
options.B: They only work against bacteria, not viruses
options.C: They contain live parts that mutate inside the body
options.D: They produce a weaker immune response because the germ is dead

explanation: Since dead germs cannot multiply inside the body, the immune system needs extra doses to build long-term memory. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h2)

question: When is the BCG vaccine usually given to a newborn in Nigeria?
explanation: BCG is given right after birth to protect babies against serious childhood forms of tuberculosis. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h3)

question: A baby is brought to the clinic at 10 weeks old and only received birth vaccines. Which ones are due today?

options.B: BCG booster and Hepatitis B second dose
options.C: Measles, Yellow Fever, and Meningitis vaccine

explanation: The 10-week clinic visit covers the second round of infant immunizations, which follows the first set given at six weeks. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h3)

question: What is the correct temperature range for storing routine vaccines in a clinic fridge?
explanation: Keeping vaccines between two and eight degrees Celsius protects them from losing their strength. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h4)

question: What happens to vaccines like Pentavalent and Hepatitis B if they get accidentally frozen?

options.A: They become stronger and cause fevers
options.C: They freeze into crystals but stay completely safe to use
options.D: They lose their strength and do not work anymore

explanation: Freezing ruins the special aluminum mix inside these vaccines, destroying their ability to protect against disease. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h4)

question: How long should a nurse watch a patient right after giving an injection?
explanation: Severe allergic reactions usually happen quickly, so keeping the patient close for a short time is a necessary safety step. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h5)

question: An abscess forms at an injection site because dirty equipment was used. What type of reaction is this?
explanation: Infections or abscesses caused by poor injection steps or unclean tools are grouped as program or operational errors. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h5)

question: Which situation means a patient should never get that vaccine ever again?

options.A: A mild cold with a low fever
options.B: A family history of minor fever-related seizures
options.C: A severe, life-threatening allergic reaction to a past dose
options.D: Low birth weight in a stable baby

explanation: A serious allergy means the vaccine is unsafe to repeat. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h6)

question: What should a nurse do if an infant scheduled for shots has a mild cold?

options.A: Send the baby to the emergency ward
options.B: Wait until the cold is completely gone before giving any shots
options.D: Double the vaccine dose to fight the cold

explanation: A minor illness without fever or complications does not stop the body from responding well to a vaccine. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h6)

question: What is the best way for a nurse to handle vaccine fears in a community?

options.A: Threaten parents with trouble from the law
options.B: Ignore what people are saying and focus only on clinic forms
options.C: Tell parents to obey without asking questions
options.D: Listen respectfully to worries and explain facts clearly

explanation: Showing patience and explaining things clearly helps build trust and addresses parent concerns. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h7)

question: A mother is scared a vaccine will give her baby the actual illness. How should the nurse answer?

options.A: Explain that vaccines contain dead or weakened germs that cannot cause the full disease
options.B: Tell her that only adults get sick from vaccines
options.C: Agree with her and tell her to skip the shots
options.D: Tell her that vaccines are just chemical drugs, not germs

explanation: Explaining how vaccines are made helps parents understand that the shot is safe and cannot give them the infection. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h7)
